title: Given a tree and a non-empty list of employees/nodes (which may contain duplicates), return the deepest node whose subtree contains ALL of them. Deduplicate the targets, then in postorder count target nodes in each subtree (including the root), returning the deepest node containing every distinct target in O(N + K) time and O(N) space. Follow-up: if the tree is fixed but you receive thousands of queries, separate preprocessing cost from per-query cost using an Euler-tour and sparse table for O(1) LCA per pair.
shortTitle: Lowest Common Ancestor of N Nodes — deepest node whose subtree contains all targets

s1_definition.profdef: The Lowest Common Ancestor of a set of nodes generalizes the two-node case to any number of targets. After deduplicating the targets into a set, a single post-order traversal counts, for each node, how many distinct targets appear in its subtree including itself; the deepest node whose subtree count equals the number of distinct targets is the answer. For many queries over a fixed tree, you preprocess once with an Euler tour and a sparse table so each pairwise LCA is answered in constant time.
s1_definition.analogy: Compliance flags not two but a whole group of employees in one suspicious transaction ring, and HR needs the lowest-level manager who oversees every one of them. Starting from the bottom up, each manager counts how many of the flagged people fall under them. The deepest manager whose count reaches the full group size is the common boss of the entire ring.
s1_definition.oneliner: Deduplicate the targets, count distinct targets per subtree in post-order, and return the deepest node whose subtree contains all of them.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Lowest Common Ancestor of a set of nodes generalizes the two-node case to any number of targets. After deduplicating the targets into a set, a single post-order traversal counts, for each node, how many distinct targets appear in its subtree including itself; the deepest node whose subtree count equals the number of distinct targets is the answer. For many queries over a fixed tree, you preprocess once with an Euler tour and a sparse table so each pairwise LCA is answered in constant time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Compliance flags not two but a whole group of employees in one suspicious transaction ring, and HR needs the lowest-level manager who oversees every one of them. Starting from the bottom up, each manager counts how many of the flagged people fall under them. The deepest manager whose count reaches the full group size is the common boss of the entire ring.

**One line to remember:** Deduplicate the targets, count distinct targets per subtree in post-order, and return the deepest node whose subtree contains all of them.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-node algorithm does not directly extend by pairing, so the clean approach counts coverage. First you deduplicate the targets into a set, because duplicates should not inflate the required count. For example: `Set<Node> targets = new HashSet<>(list);`.

You then run a post-order traversal where each node returns how many distinct targets its subtree contains. A node's count is the sum of its children's counts plus one if the node itself is a target. For example: `int count = leftCount + rightCount + (targets.contains(node) ? 1 : 0);`.

The lowest common ancestor is the deepest node whose count equals the total number of distinct targets. Because post-order visits children before parents, the first node you encounter in post-order whose count reaches the full target size is the deepest such node. For example, you record the node the moment `count == targets.size()` and it has not been recorded yet.

This runs in time proportional to the number of nodes plus the number of targets, using set membership checks that are constant on average, and space proportional to the number of nodes for the recursion and the set. This is the answer the question explicitly asks for.

The follow-up changes the economics. If the tree is fixed and you answer thousands of queries, repeating a linear traversal per query is wasteful. You preprocess with an Euler tour, which records nodes in the order visited during a depth-first walk along with their depths, and build a sparse table for range-minimum queries over that depth array. Then the lowest common ancestor of any pair is the shallowest node in the Euler tour between their first occurrences, answerable in constant time after order-n-log-n preprocessing. For a set of nodes, you fold pairwise: the LCA of the whole set is the LCA of the running result with the next node, so k nodes need k-minus-one constant-time pair queries. A senior nuance is recognizing this preprocessing-versus-per-query tradeoff explicitly, because it is the heart of the follow-up.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a fraud ring investigation flags a group of employees, possibly with duplicates from multiple reports, and compliance needs the single lowest-level manager who oversees the entire group. This is exactly how LCA of N nodes works — the deepest node whose subtree covers all distinct targets.

Problem 2 — During a large investigation the same org tree is queried thousands of times for different groups, so a per-query linear scan is too slow. This is exactly why the follow-up separates one-time preprocessing from fast per-query lookups using an Euler tour and sparse table.

The mini-project builds an `EmployeeNode` class, a `MultiLcaService` with a post-order counting LCA over a deduplicated set and logging, and a runnable demo over a flagged group.

sections.s5_journey:
The input flagged group is Meena, Priya, Rajesh, and Priya again. After deduplication the distinct targets are Meena, Priya, and Rajesh, so the required count is three.

Step 1: The post-order traversal starts descending. At Meena, a leaf and a target, the count is one. Meena's parent Rajesh is also a target, and Rajesh's left subtree reported one for Meena, so Rajesh's count is one for Meena plus one for Rajesh himself, which is two. Rajesh's count two is not yet three.

Step 2: Priya is a leaf and a target, so Priya's count is one.

Step 3: RegionHead sums its children: Rajesh's subtree contributed two and Priya contributed one, and RegionHead itself is not a target, so RegionHead's count is three. This equals the required distinct count, and since this is the first node in post-order to reach three, RegionHead is recorded as the result.

Step 4: AuditHead's subtree contains Arjun, who is not in this group, so its count is zero. CEO sums RegionHead's three and AuditHead's zero for a total of three, which also equals the required count, but the result was already set to the deeper RegionHead, so it is not overwritten.

Step 5: The answer for the first group is RegionHead, the deepest manager overseeing all of Meena, Priya, and Rajesh. For the second group Meena and Arjun, Meena sits under RegionHead on the left and Arjun under AuditHead on the right, so only CEO's subtree reaches the full count, making CEO the answer.

```text
2026-10-26T18:50:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Fraud Ring Common Manager (LCA of N)
2026-10-26T18:50:00Z [INFO] Lowest manager overseeing the entire flagged group is RegionHead
2026-10-26T18:50:00Z [INFO] Lowest manager overseeing the entire flagged group is CEO
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Targets (dedup): {Meena, Priya, Rajesh}  → need count 3

                 CEO (3)
               /        \
        RegionHead(3)   AuditHead(0)
          /      \            \
     Rajesh(2)  Priya(1)     Arjun(0)
        │
     Meena(1)

  Post-order counts bubble up:
    Meena=1 → Rajesh=1+1=2 → Priya=1
    RegionHead=2+1+0=3  ← FIRST to reach 3 (deepest) = ANSWER
    CEO=3+0=3  (already recorded deeper node, not overwritten)
```

```text
  │  - result: EmployeeNode               │ deepest full-cover
  │  + lcaOfMany(root, nodes): Node       │ O(N + K) time, O(N) space
  │  - countTargets(node): int            │ post-order count
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Single query:  count distinct targets per subtree; deepest == K.
  Many queries:  preprocess O(N log N); each pair LCA O(1);
                 fold set: lca = lca(lca(...lca(a,b),c)...), K-1 pairs.

  Contract: non-empty targets; returns deepest node covering all.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Lowest Common Ancestor of a whole set of nodes generalizes the two-node case, and the clean approach is counting coverage rather than pairing. I first deduplicate the targets into a set, because duplicates must not inflate the required count. Then I run a single post-order traversal where each node returns how many distinct targets live in its subtree, which is the sum of its children's counts plus one if the node itself is a target. The answer is the deepest node whose count equals the number of distinct targets, and because post-order visits children before parents, the first node I see reach the full count is guaranteed to be the deepest such node. This runs in time proportional to the number of nodes plus targets and space proportional to the tree.

The follow-up is where the senior thinking shows, because it changes the economics entirely. If the tree is fixed but I answer thousands of queries, repeating a linear traversal each time is wasteful, so I separate one-time preprocessing from cheap per-query cost. I build an Euler tour, which records the nodes in the order a depth-first walk visits them along with their depths, and a sparse table for range-minimum queries over that depth array. After that order-n-log-n preprocessing, the ancestor of any pair is the shallowest node in the tour between their first occurrences, answered in constant time.

For a set rather than a pair, I fold pairwise, because the ancestor of the whole set is the ancestor of the running result with the next node, so k targets need k-minus-one constant-time pair queries. Explicitly naming this preprocessing-versus-per-query tradeoff is the point of the follow-up, and it is the same reasoning that drives caching and indexing decisions in real systems.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this in a fraud ring investigation. Compliance flags a group of employees, sometimes with duplicates from multiple reports, and we need the single lowest-level manager overseeing the entire group. The counting traversal answers one investigation directly, and when a large case fired thousands of group queries against the same fixed org tree, I switched to the Euler-tour and sparse-table preprocessing so each query resolved almost instantly.
